v-collocation-01.reason: 'Meet a deadline' is the fixed collocation; match, catch and suit do not combine with 'deadline'.
v-collocation-01.why: A staple business collocation most test-takers know; the distractors are 'fit'-type verbs that fail with 'deadline'.

v-collocation-02.reason: 'Heavy traffic' is the standard collocation; strong, hard and large traffic are not used for congestion.
v-collocation-02.why: One of the first collocations learners meet, and the delay clause confirms it, so it reads like a textbook drill.
v-collocation-02.fix: If the set does not need another easy anchor, test a less basic collocation in the same frame, e.g. 'Because of ______ road repairs on the bridge, ...' with (A) extensive (B) spacious (C) wide (D) roomy.

v-collocation-03.reason: 'Place an order' is the fixed business collocation.
v-collocation-03.why: A heavily practised TOEIC collocation; set, lay and position are plausible 'put' verbs but none pairs with 'order'.

v-collocation-04.reason: 'Keep a close eye on' is the idiom; 'take a close look' exists but 'take a close eye' does not.
v-collocation-04.why: Needs the whole idiom, and 'take' lures anyone who half-remembers 'take a close look'.

v-collocation-05.reason: 'Strike a balance between' is the fixed expression.
v-collocation-05.why: Only the fixed phrase decides, but punch, beat and knock are plainly out of register in business prose, so the item reduces to picking the one formal 'hit' verb.
v-collocation-05.fix: Use distractors that collocate with other business nouns so they look usable, e.g. (A) strike (B) pull (C) run (D) lift.

v-collocation-06.reason: 'Overwhelming majority' is the standard collocation; 'overriding' goes with concern or priority.
v-collocation-06.why: All four look alike and fit the article 'an', so the collocation alone decides, with 'overriding' as the strongest lure.

v-synonym-01.reason: Transitive 'raise' takes 'its prices' as object; rise and arise are intransitive and arouse is used for feelings.
v-synonym-01.why: Only the rise/raise contrast is live; arise and arouse are dismissed at a glance and make the set look like a grammar-book list of confusables.
v-synonym-01.fix: Make all four options mean 'go up' so only transitivity decides: (A) raise (B) rise (C) climb (D) grow.

v-synonym-02.reason: Only 'tell' takes a person object followed by a that-clause; say, speak and talk would need 'to' or a different pattern.
v-synonym-02.why: The say/tell/speak/talk set is a basic ESL grammar drill, not a business vocabulary item, and the opening 'Yesterday' is unlike real Part 5 sentences.
v-synonym-02.fix: Use (A) informed (B) announced (C) explained (D) mentioned (key A) and start with the subject: 'The facilities manager ______ the staff that the building will close early on Friday for maintenance.'

v-synonym-03.reason: 'Reply' needs 'to'; 'answer' is transitive (answered my email), and contact and inform need a person object.
v-synonym-03.why: 'Answered' is equally attractive in meaning, so the preposition decides; the contraction and first-person 'my email' read like a personal note rather than a Part 5 sentence.
v-synonym-03.fix: Rewrite as 'Ms. Pell has not yet ______ to the client's e-mail about moving the budget meeting to next week.' and keep the options.

v-synonym-04.reason: 'Comprise' takes the parts as its direct object; 'consist' needs 'of', and compose and constitute run the other way (the parts compose the whole).
v-synonym-04.why: All four share a meaning, so only each verb's direction and complement pattern decides, and 'consists' traps many learners.

v-synonym-05.reason: 'Notify' takes the person or office being told as object; notice means see, and announce and declare take the message as object.
v-synonym-05.why: 'Notice' is a look-alike trap, and announce and declare are right in meaning but wrong in object.

v-synonym-06.reason: A lease is extended in time; expand, enlarge and stretch describe size.
v-synonym-06.why: Extend versus expand is a known pair, but 'for another two years' makes the time sense obvious.

v-business-01.reason: An itinerary lists flight times and hotels; an agenda lists topics for a meeting.
v-business-01.why: Needs the lower-frequency word 'itinerary', with 'agenda' as a tempting schedule-type near-miss.

v-business-02.reason: 'Payable within 30 days' identifies a bill, i.e. an invoice.
v-business-02.why: Receipt and estimate stay plausible until 'payable' rules them out, so the decisive cue comes late in the sentence.

v-business-03.why: 'Until next Thursday' gives the meaning away and the distractors are wrong at a glance.

v-business-04.reason: Money is 'deducted from' a salary; 'reduced' would need the salary as its subject.
v-business-04.why: 'Reduced' is a meaning-level trap, so knowing 'deduct from' decides.

v-business-05.reason: Staff are 'reimbursed' for expenses they paid themselves.
v-business-05.why: 'Rewarded' is a tempting near-miss, and the key is a core but mid-frequency business verb.

v-business-06.reason: A company 'absorbs' a cost when it pays the cost itself instead of passing it on.
v-business-06.why: 'Absorb the cost' is a less frequent business sense of a common word; the others can be eliminated only by a learner who trusts that sense.

v-family-01.reason: 'Considerable' means large; 'considerate' means thoughtful and describes people.
v-family-01.why: A classic considerate/considerable trap, but 'a considerable amount' is so frequent that most test-takers recognise it.

v-family-02.reason: 'Sensitive information' means confidential information; 'sensible' means reasonable.
v-family-02.why: 'Sensible' is a well-known trap, and 'salaries' plus 'locked' make the confidential sense clear.

v-family-03.reason: 'Their respective regions' means each person's own region.
v-family-03.why: All three distractors are same-root adjectives that learners know better, so only knowing 'respective' decides.

v-family-04.reason: 'Industrious' means hard-working and describes people; the other three relate to industry.
v-family-04.why: The context calls for a personal quality, which removes the three industry words for anyone who knows 'industrious'.

v-family-05.why: 'Comprehensive' is the more familiar word and a strong trap, while 'plain language' points to understandability.

v-family-06.reason: 'Every imaginable size' means every size one can think of; imaginative means creative and imaginary means unreal.
v-family-06.why: Needs separating three real -ive/-ary/-able adjectives, with 'imaginative' as a strong lure.

overall: All 24 items have a single defensible key in both British and American usage; I found no ambiguous items, and the closest near-misses (agenda for itinerary, answered for replied, take for keep a close eye) fail on standard usage. The band mix I judge is 8 easy, 12 medium and 4 hard, which is a believable spread, though a real set would probably have a somewhat heavier hard end; I rated vsToeic against real vocabulary items in general and band as the item's place within a real set. The hard items are all commonly-confused-word types (comprises, absorb, respective, imaginable); the set has no hard item where four same-part-of-speech words all fit in isolation and only the context decides, and no adverb vocabulary items, both of which I judge are common in real Part 5. Several near-synonym items (raise, told, replied, comprises, notify) are decided by verb pattern (transitivity, a required preposition, what the object is) rather than meaning, which pushes them toward grammar. Wording is mostly close to real items (short workplace sentences, named staff, notices and invoices); resemblance is weakest in v-synonym-02 (say/tell drill), v-synonym-03 (contraction and first person) and items whose distractors are wrong at a glance (v-collocation-02, v-collocation-05, v-synonym-01).
